title: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
subject: Medicine
summary: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease affecting multiple organ systems. It is characterized by inflammation, autoantibody production, and diverse clinical manifestations. Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical features and specific laboratory tests.

sections.p: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory disease that can affect virtually any organ system. It is characterized by the production of autoantibodies, particularly antinuclear antibodies (ANA). Diagnosis is clinical, supported by laboratory findings, and often follows established classification criteria to ensure consistency.
b: SLE is defined by immune system dysregulation leading to widespread inflammation.
Diagnosis requires a combination of clinical features (e.g., rash, arthritis, serositis, renal involvement, cytopenias) and specific autoantibodies.
The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) or Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics (SLICC) criteria are commonly used for classification.

sections.p: SLE severity varies widely, from mild skin and joint involvement to severe, life-threatening organ damage. Staging is not a formal system like cancer, but rather an assessment of active disease burden and cumulative organ damage. This guides treatment intensity and prognosis.
b: Mild SLE: primarily skin, joints, and serositis, often managed with antimalarials and NSAIDs.
Moderate SLE: involvement of one or more major organs (e.g., kidneys, CNS, haematological) that is not immediately life-threatening.
Severe SLE: active, life-threatening involvement of major organs, requiring aggressive immunosuppression.
Disease activity indices (e.g., SLEDAI) are used to quantify current disease activity, while damage indices (e.g., SLICC/ACR Damage Index) assess irreversible organ damage.

sections.p: The exact cause of SLE is unknown, but it is believed to result from a complex interplay of genetic predisposition, environmental triggers, and hormonal factors. It is more common in women and certain ethnic groups.
b: Genetic predisposition: specific HLA alleles and other gene variants increase susceptibility.
Environmental triggers: ultraviolet (UV) light exposure, certain infections (e.g., Epstein-Barr virus), and some medications can precipitate or exacerbate SLE.
Hormonal factors: estrogen is thought to play a role, explaining the higher prevalence in women of childbearing age.
Immune dysregulation: defective clearance of apoptotic cells and activation of innate and adaptive immune responses lead to autoantibody production.

sections.p: SLE can present with a wide array of symptoms, making diagnosis challenging. Common presentations involve the skin, joints, kidneys, and haematological system. Symptoms can wax and wane, often presenting as flares.
b: General: fatigue, fever, weight loss.
Skin: malar (butterfly) rash, discoid rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers.
Musculoskeletal: polyarthritis (often symmetrical, non-erosive), arthralgia, myalgia.
Renal: proteinuria, haematuria, hypertension (lupus nephritis, a major cause of morbidity).
Haematological: anaemia (haemolytic or chronic disease), leukopenia, thrombocytopenia.
Serositis: pleurisy, pericarditis (causing chest pain, shortness of breath).
Neurological: seizures, psychosis, cognitive dysfunction, headaches (neuropsychiatric lupus).
Cardiovascular: Libman-Sacks endocarditis (sterile vegetations), accelerated atherosclerosis.
Gastrointestinal: abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, pancreatitis, hepatitis.

sections.p: Investigations aim to support the diagnosis, assess organ involvement, and monitor disease activity. In low-resource settings, prioritize basic tests before considering more specialized ones.

t.b: Screens for cytopenias (leukopenia, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, anaemia). Low counts are common in SLE. If unavailable, clinical assessment of pallor, bruising, and infection risk is crucial.

Measures inflammation. ESR is often elevated in active SLE, while CRP may be normal or mildly elevated unless there is an infection or serositis. If unavailable, clinical signs of inflammation (fever, swelling) are key.

Screens for proteinuria and haematuria, indicating lupus nephritis. Red cell casts are highly suggestive of glomerulonephritis. If unavailable, clinical signs of oedema, hypertension, and reduced urine output should raise suspicion.
Assesses kidney function. Elevated levels suggest renal impairment, often due to lupus nephritis. If unavailable, monitor urine output and clinical signs of uraemia.

A highly sensitive screening test for SLE. A positive ANA (usually titre 1:80 or more) is present in over 95% of SLE patients. A negative ANA makes SLE highly unlikely. If unavailable, rely more heavily on clinical criteria and other available autoantibodies.

Highly specific for SLE and often correlates with disease activity, especially lupus nephritis. A rising titre can indicate a flare. If unavailable, monitor clinical signs of renal disease and other organ involvement.
Often consumed and low during active SLE, particularly with renal involvement. Low levels indicate immune complex activity. If unavailable, clinical assessment of disease activity is paramount.

t.a: Antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta2-glycoprotein I)
t.b: Screens for antiphospholipid syndrome, which can coexist with SLE and cause thrombosis and recurrent pregnancy loss. If unavailable, a history of recurrent clots or miscarriages should raise suspicion.

Definitively diagnoses lupus nephritis, classifies its type, and assesses severity and chronicity, guiding specific treatment. This is a specialized test and may not be available in all low-resource settings; clinical judgment and response to empiric treatment become critical.

sections.p: Recognizing red flags and potential complications is crucial for timely intervention and preventing irreversible organ damage or death. SLE can affect any organ, leading to diverse severe outcomes.
b: Lupus nephritis: can lead to end-stage renal disease.
Neuropsychiatric lupus: seizures, psychosis, stroke, cognitive impairment.
Cardiovascular disease: accelerated atherosclerosis, pericarditis, myocarditis, Libman-Sacks endocarditis.
Infections: increased risk due to immunosuppression and disease itself.
Thrombosis: due to antiphospholipid antibodies, leading to DVT, PE, stroke.
Pulmonary haemorrhage: a rare but life-threatening complication.
Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome: widespread microthrombosis affecting multiple organs.

sections.p: Management of SLE is individualized, aiming to control inflammation, prevent flares, minimize organ damage, and improve quality of life. Treatment depends on disease severity and organ involvement.
b: General measures: sun protection, smoking cessation, regular exercise, healthy diet, vaccinations (avoid live vaccines if on immunosuppressants).
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs): for mild arthralgia, myalgia, and serositis. Use cautiously due to potential renal and gastrointestinal side effects.

Antimalarials (e.g., hydroxychloroquine): cornerstone of SLE treatment for most patients, reducing flares, improving skin and joint symptoms, and preventing organ damage. Requires regular ophthalmological screening.
Corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone): used for acute flares and moderate-to-severe organ involvement. Doses are tapered once disease activity is controlled to minimize side effects.

Immunosuppressants (e.g., azathioprine, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide): used for moderate-to-severe disease, especially lupus nephritis, to spare steroids and achieve long-term remission. Cyclophosphamide is often reserved for severe, life-threatening disease.
Biologics (e.g., belimumab, rituximab): newer agents for refractory disease or specific manifestations, often not available in low-resource settings.
Specific organ management: e.g., antihypertensives for renal involvement, anticoagulation for thrombosis.

sections.p: Regular follow-up is essential to monitor disease activity, detect complications early, and adjust treatment. Patient education on self-management and adherence is key to preventing flares.
b: Regular clinical assessment: monitor symptoms, physical examination for signs of organ involvement.
Laboratory monitoring: FBC, ESR, CRP, renal function, urine analysis, complement levels, anti-dsDNA titres.
Screening for complications: e.g., bone density for osteoporosis, cardiovascular risk assessment.
Patient education: importance of medication adherence, sun protection, recognizing flare symptoms.
Family planning: counsel women of childbearing age on safe contraception and pregnancy planning due to risks associated with SLE and certain medications.

sections.p: The diverse presentation of SLE means it can mimic many other conditions, leading to diagnostic delays. Distinguishing features are crucial.
b: Rheumatoid Arthritis: SLE polyarthritis is typically non-erosive, unlike RA. RA usually has positive anti-CCP antibodies and rheumatoid factor (though RF can be positive in SLE).

Drug-induced Lupus: often presents with arthralgia, myalgia, and serositis, and a positive ANA. However, anti-dsDNA is usually negative, and symptoms resolve upon drug discontinuation (e.g., hydralazine, procainamide).
Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD): shares features of SLE, scleroderma, and polymyositis. Characterized by high titres of anti-U1-RNP antibodies.
Infections (e.g., HIV, TB, malaria): can cause fever, cytopenias, and organ involvement. Differentiating requires careful history, physical exam, and specific infectious disease testing.
Other autoimmune diseases: Sjogren's syndrome, systemic sclerosis, vasculitis can have overlapping symptoms and autoantibodies.

sections.p: Laboratory results in SLE can sometimes be misleading, requiring careful clinical correlation. A single test result should not be interpreted in isolation.
b: Positive ANA: can be present in healthy individuals (especially low titres), other autoimmune diseases, and chronic infections. Not specific for SLE.
Normal CRP: unlike many inflammatory conditions, CRP may not be significantly elevated in active SLE unless there is serositis or infection, while ESR is usually high.
Negative anti-dsDNA: about 5-10% of SLE patients may be anti-dsDNA negative, especially those with mild disease or specific organ involvement (e.g., skin).
Low complement levels: can also be seen in infections or other immune complex diseases, not exclusively SLE.
Cytopenias: can be caused by many conditions, including infections, nutritional deficiencies, or drug side effects, not just SLE.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe headache, seizures, or new neurological deficits.
Acute shortness of breath, chest pain, or rapid heart rate.
New onset or worsening severe abdominal pain.
Rapidly progressive kidney failure (decreased urine output, severe oedema).
High fever with signs of infection (e.g., cough, painful urination) in an immunosuppressed patient.
New onset of severe bleeding or bruising.

faq.a: No, SLE is a chronic disease with no known cure, but it can be effectively managed with medication to control symptoms and prevent organ damage.
No, SLE is an autoimmune disease and is not contagious. It cannot be spread from person to person.
A lupus flare is a period of increased disease activity, where symptoms worsen or new symptoms appear, often requiring adjustment of medication.

exam: A 28-year-old woman presents with a malar rash, joint pain, and fatigue. Her ANA is positive. What is your next diagnostic step, and why? — Next, order anti-dsDNA antibodies and complement levels (C3, C4) to confirm SLE and assess potential renal involvement. Also, a urine dipstick and FBC to screen for nephritis and cytopenias.

You suspect lupus nephritis in a patient with SLE. What investigations would you prioritize in a low-resource setting, and what would each tell you? — Prioritize urine dipstick and microscopy (for proteinuria, haematuria, casts), serum creatinine and urea (for renal function), and FBC (for anaemia, cytopenias). If available, anti-dsDNA and complement levels would further support the diagnosis and assess activity.

A patient with known SLE on hydroxychloroquine develops new onset shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. What are your immediate concerns, and how would you differentiate them? — Consider serositis (pleuritis), pulmonary embolism (especially if antiphospholipid antibodies are present), or infection. Differentiate with clinical assessment, chest X-ray, and if available, D-dimer and ECG. Auscultate for pleural rub or signs of consolidation.

What are the key differences in joint involvement between SLE and Rheumatoid Arthritis? — SLE polyarthritis is typically non-erosive and migratory, while RA is often erosive, deforming, and symmetrical, primarily affecting small joints of hands and feet. Serologically, RA has anti-CCP and RF, while SLE has ANA and anti-dsDNA.

A patient with SLE is prescribed prednisone for a flare. What are the important counseling points regarding this medication, particularly in a low-resource setting? — Counsel on adherence, gradual tapering (never stop abruptly), potential side effects (weight gain, mood changes, increased infection risk, osteoporosis), and the importance of calcium/vitamin D supplementation if available. Emphasize infection prevention.

You have a patient with SLE who is pregnant. What are the key considerations for managing her condition during pregnancy? — Monitor disease activity closely, ensure medications are safe for pregnancy (e.g., hydroxychloroquine is safe, mycophenolate mofetil is contraindicated), screen for pre-eclampsia and fetal growth restriction, and monitor for antiphospholipid syndrome if present due to increased risk of thrombosis and miscarriage.

What are the 'red flags' that would prompt you to admit an SLE patient to the hospital immediately? — New seizures or severe neurological deficits, acute severe shortness of breath or chest pain, rapidly worsening renal function, severe cytopenias with bleeding or infection, or signs of catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic exam can uncover the multisystem nature of SLE and differentiate it from mimics, while recognising the limits of bedside testing.
b: Onset and duration of rash, joint pain, fatigue; ask about photosensitivity and seasonal variation.
History of oral ulcers, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, haematuria, foamy urine, or swelling.
Medication and herbal exposure (e.g., procainamide, hydralazine, minocycline) that can induce lupus‑like syndrome.
Pregnancy status, contraceptive use, and recent infections (especially viral).
Family history of autoimmune disease and ethnic background (higher prevalence in African descent).
Review constitutional symptoms: fever, weight loss, night sweats.
Ask about thrombotic events, miscarriages, or antiphospholipid syndrome features.

t.b: Inspect for malar rash (spares nasolabial folds), discoid plaques, photosensitive lesions; elicit by gentle pressure to assess tenderness. Positive rash supports cutaneous lupus; cannot determine serology or activity level.
Palpate wrists, MCP, PIP, knees for swelling, warmth, tenderness; assess range of motion. Symmetric non‑erosive arthritis suggests SLE; bedside cannot grade radiographic erosions.
Auscultate heart for pericardial rub and lungs for pleural friction rub; pericardial friction indicates serositis. Bedside cannot quantify effusion size.
Inspect for oedema, palpate for flank tenderness, assess blood pressure. Presence of oedema raises suspicion for lupus nephritis; bedside cannot differentiate type of renal pathology.
Brief mental status, cranial nerve testing, motor strength, and sensory exam. Seizure or psychosis history suggests neuro‑lupus; bedside cannot localise CNS lesions.
Check for livedo reticularis, digital ulcers, or peripheral pulses. Positive livedo may point to antiphospholipid syndrome; bedside cannot confirm antiphospholipid antibodies.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Laboratory and imaging studies answer specific diagnostic and activity questions; when a test is unavailable, use clinical surrogates or refer to a higher‑level centre.
b: ANA by indirect immunofluorescence – screening; titre ≥1:80 is positive. A negative ANA essentially excludes SLE.
Anti‑dsDNA – organ‑specific marker; titres >100 IU/mL correlate with renal activity; falling titres suggest response.
Anti‑Sm – highly specific for SLE; presence supports diagnosis but not activity.
Complement C3/C4 – low levels (<0.9 g/L C3 or <0.1 g/L C4) indicate active immune‑complex disease.
Urinalysis – protein ≥0.5 g/day, cellular casts, haematuria; suggests lupus nephritis.
Renal function – serum creatinine, eGFR; rising creatinine signals renal flare.
Complete blood count – anaemia, leukopenia (<4 ×10⁹/L), thrombocytopenia (<150 ×10⁹/L) are haematologic criteria.
ESR/CRP – ESR often markedly raised; CRP may be normal unless infection.
SLEDAI‑2K – calculates disease activity; ≥4 mild, ≥6 moderate, ≥12 high activity.
Kidney biopsy – gold standard for classifying lupus nephritis (ISN/RPS classes). If unavailable, treat based on proteinuria >1 g/day and rising creatinine.
Antiphospholipid antibodies – lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG/IgM; prolonged aPTT in vitro, paradoxical thrombosis in vivo.
Chest X‑ray – pleural effusion or pulmonary infiltrates; if not available, use bedside ultrasound.

t.b: Answers: does the patient meet the entry criterion for 2019 EULAR/ACR classification? A negative result essentially rules out SLE; no further serology needed.
Answers: how to gauge renal activity? Use complement levels, proteinuria, and rising creatinine as surrogates; consider referral for biopsy if possible.
Answers: is there active immune‑complex disease? Low C3/C4 supports activity; if unavailable, rely on clinical flare signs and anti‑dsDNA trends.
Answers: is there renal involvement? 2+ (~100 mg/dL) suggests >0.5 g/day protein; confirm with quantitative protein/creatinine ratio; if lab unavailable, treat as possible nephritis.
Answers: risk of thrombosis/obstetric loss? In vitro prolongation of aPTT; manage with anticoagulation despite paradoxical lab finding.

sections.p: Classification uses the 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria; severity is graded by organ involvement and activity scores.
b: Entry criterion: ANA ≥1:80 by immunofluorescence.
Add points from clinical domains (e.g., acute cutaneous lupus 6, joint involvement 6, renal proteinuria >0.5 g/day 4).
Add points from immunologic domain (anti‑dsDNA 6, low complement 4, anti‑Sm 6).
Total ≥10 points classifies as SLE.

Stage severity by organ involvement: mild (skin/joints only), moderate (single major organ without life‑threatening features), severe (life‑threatening organ disease, CNS, renal class III/IV, pulmonary haemorrhage).
Activity measured by SLEDAI‑2K: ≥4 mild, ≥6 moderate, ≥12 high activity.
Damage assessed by SLICC/ACR Damage Index (once disease duration >6 months).

sections.p: Several disorders mimic SLE; careful history, targeted tests and organ‑specific clues separate them.

t.b: Points: exposure to hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid; usually antihistone antibodies positive, anti‑dsDNA negative; resolves after drug withdrawal.
Points: high‑titer anti‑U1 RNP, prominent Raynaud’s, myositis; overlapping features but anti‑Sm absent.
Points: heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, muscle weakness, CK elevation; skin findings differ from malar rash; anti‑Mi‑2 or anti‑MDA5 positive.
Points: erosive changes on X‑ray, rheumatoid factor/anti‑CCP positive, symmetric erosive polyarthritis; SLE arthritis is non‑erosive.
Points: skin thickening, sclerodactyly, Raynaud’s, anti‑Scl‑70; renal crisis possible but lacks ANA pattern of SLE.

t.a: Infection‑related immune complex disease (e.g., post‑streptococcal GN)
t.b: Points: recent streptococcal infection, low complement C3 only, ASO titre high; renal biopsy shows subepithelial ‘humps’ rather than full‑house immunofluorescence.

sections.p: A structured ladder guides treatment from basic control to organ‑specific immunosuppression, with clear triggers for escalation and referral.
b: 1. Confirm diagnosis, document disease activity (SLEDAI‑2K) and organ involvement.
2. Start hydroxychloroquine for all patients unless contraindicated; monitor retinal health.
3. Add NSAID for mild arthritis or serositis, avoiding in renal failure or active GI ulcer.
5. Severe organ threat (life‑threatening nephritis, CNS, vasculitis) – give high‑dose IV methylprednisolone then switch to oral taper; add cyclophosphamide IV or mycophenolate as induction.
6. If disease remains active despite conventional agents, refer for biologic therapy (rituximab or belimumab) and rheumatology input.
7. Monitor labs (CBC, renal, liver, complement, anti‑dsDNA) every 4–6 weeks initially, then 3‑monthly; adjust therapy based on trends.
8. Escalate to specialist centre if refractory disease, severe organ damage, pregnancy, or drug toxicity develops.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse effects, drug‑drug interactions and practical actions to mitigate toxicity.
b: Hydroxychloroquine – retinal toxicity; obtain baseline and annual fundus exam, stop if visual changes.
Prednisone – hyperglycaemia, hypertension, osteoporosis, infection risk; give calcium/vit D, screen glucose, taper promptly.
Mycophenolate – GI upset, leukopenia, teratogenic; monitor CBC, avoid in pregnancy, switch to azathioprine if pregnant.
Azathioprine – TPMT deficiency risk; test TPMT activity before start, monitor CBC and liver enzymes.
Cyclophosphamide – hemorrhagic cystitis, infertility, secondary malignancy; give adequate hydration, consider mesna, counsel on contraception.
Rituximab – infusion reactions, hepatitis B reactivation; pre‑medicate with antihistamine/steroid, screen HBV, vaccinate before therapy.
NSAIDs – renal impairment, GI bleed; use lowest effective dose, co‑prescribe PPI if risk, avoid in advanced CKD.

sections.p: Recognise organ‑specific complications that demand urgent escalation or admission.
b: Renal flare: rising proteinuria >0.5 g/24 h, new haematuria, rising creatinine >30 % – start high‑dose IV steroids, add cyclophosphamide or mycophenolate, admit.
Neuropsychiatric lupus: new seizures, psychosis, severe headache – high‑dose IV steroids, consider plasma exchange, urgent neurology referral.
Serositis with large effusion or tamponade signs – urgent thoracentesis/pericardiocentesis, IV steroids.
Severe cytopenias (platelets <20 ×10⁹/L, Hb <8 g/dL) with active disease – IV methylprednisolone, consider IVIG or rituximab.
Thrombotic antiphospholipid syndrome – therapeutic anticoagulation, avoid warfarin in pregnancy, refer to haematology.
Infection (fever, neutrophils <1 ×10⁹/L) while on steroids – hold immunosuppressants, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, consider IVIG if opportunistic.

sections.p: Conditions that alter presentation, laboratory interpretation or therapeutic choices.
b: HIV – overlapping cytopenias, false‑positive ANA; prefer azathioprine over mycophenolate, monitor CD4.
TB – steroids can reactivate; screen with IGRA or chest X‑ray before high‑dose steroids, treat latent TB first.
Malnutrition – low albumin may exaggerate proteinuria; supplement calories, monitor drug levels.
Pregnancy – hydroxychloroquine safe, mycophenolate contraindicated, switch to azathioprine; avoid cyclophosphamide, use low‑dose steroids only if needed.
Diabetes – steroids worsen glycaemia; intensify insulin or oral agents, monitor glucose closely.
Herbal remedies (e.g., St. John’s wort) – induce CYP enzymes, lower steroid levels; advise cessation.
Alcohol – potentiates hepatotoxicity of azathioprine, mycophenolate; limit intake.
Renal failure – adjust mycophenolate dose, avoid NSAIDs, use cyclophosphamide IV with caution.
Liver failure – avoid azathioprine, use reduced mycophenolate dose, monitor LFTs.
Very young or elderly – increased infection risk, slower steroid taper, consider lower immunosuppressive intensity.

sections.p: Tailored considerations for children, pregnant women, the elderly, HIV‑positive patients and low‑resource environments.
b: Children – growth monitoring essential; use steroid‑sparing agents early, hydroxychloroquine dose by weight, avoid cyclophosphamide if possible.
Pregnancy – continue hydroxychloroquine, switch mycophenolate to azathioprine, use low‑dose prednisone, plan delivery with rheumatology and obstetrics.
Elderly – start at lower steroid dose, monitor bone density, avoid nephrotoxic NSAIDs, consider comorbid cardiovascular risk.
HIV‑positive – prioritize agents with minimal impact on CD4 (azathioprine, hydroxychloroquine), treat opportunistic infections first, avoid high‑dose cyclophosphamide.

Low‑resource settings – use hydroxychloroquine and oral prednisone as backbone; if cyclophosphamide unavailable, use high‑dose steroids alone with close monitoring; rely on urine dipstick and creatinine for renal assessment; use clinical disease activity scores when labs limited.

sections.p: Sample questions covering bedside assessment, investigations, management and special circumstances.
b: 1. Which history question helps differentiate SLE arthritis from rheumatoid arthritis? (Answer: symmetry with non‑erosive joints, morning stiffness <30 min).
2. How do you perform a thorough skin exam for lupus rash? (Inspect face, trunk, extensor surfaces; note malar distribution sparing nasolabial folds, photosensitivity).
3. A patient has proteinuria 0.8 g/24 h and rising creatinine; what is the next step? (Answer: Admit, start IV methylprednisolone, begin induction immunosuppression).
4. When is a low complement C3/C4 result significant? (Answer: <0.9 g/L for C3 or <0.1 g/L for C4 indicates active immune‑complex disease).
5. Which drug is contraindicated in pregnancy and must be switched before conception? (Answer: Mycophenolate mofetil).
6. A lupus patient on hydroxychloroquine develops visual disturbances; what do you do? (Answer: Stop drug, arrange urgent ophthalmology review).
7. How does antiphospholipid antibody syndrome alter anticoagulation in pregnancy? (Answer: Use low‑molecular‑weight heparin, avoid warfarin).
8. In a setting without anti‑dsDNA testing, which surrogate indicates disease activity? (Answer: Rising proteinuria, falling complement, new rash).
9. What is the preferred induction regimen for class III/IV lupus nephritis when cyclophosphamide is unavailable? (Answer: High‑dose steroids plus mycophenolate mofetil).
10. A 70‑year‑old with SLE presents with fever and neutropenia; what is the immediate management? (Answer: Hold immunosuppressants, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, assess for infection source).
11. How does chronic hepatitis B affect rituximab use? (Answer: Screen, treat HBV before rituximab, monitor viral load).
12. In a low‑resource clinic, which three investigations are essential for monitoring SLE activity? (Answer: CBC, serum creatinine/eGFR, urine protein dipstick).

facts: SLE classified by 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria: ANA ≥1:80 plus ≥10 points from clinical/immunologic domains.
SLEDAI-2K score ≥4 = mild activity, ≥6 = moderate, ≥12 = high activity.
Low complement C3 <0.9 g/L or C4 <0.1 g/L indicates active immune‑complex disease.
Mycophenolate mofetil is contraindicated in pregnancy; switch to azathioprine if needed.
Cyclophosphamide is generally contraindicated in pregnancy; use only if benefits outweigh risks.
Belimumab is first biologic escalation after steroids and hydroxychloroquine.
Renal failure is a leading cause of morbidity; cardiovascular disease is leading cause of mortality in SLE.

vivas.q: Define SLE and explain the 2019 EULAR/ACR classification criteria.
vivas.a: SLE is a systemic autoimmune disease. 2019 EULAR/ACR requires ANA ≥1:80 plus ≥10 points from clinical/immunologic domains.

vivas.q: What is the significance of low C3/C4 in a patient with suspected lupus nephritis?
vivas.a: Low C3 (<0.9 g/L) or C4 (<0.1 g/L) indicates active immune‑complex deposition and predicts renal flare.

vivas.q: A 28‑year‑old woman with malar rash, arthralgia, and fatigue has a positive ANA. What is the next step?
vivas.a: Order anti‑dsDNA, complement levels, and renal screen (urine protein/creatinine).

vivas.q: Why is hydroxychloroquine preferred over azathioprine in stable SLE?
vivas.a: Hydroxychloroquine reduces flares, is safe in pregnancy, and has fewer myelosuppressive effects.

vivas.q: Explain the difference between SLE and rheumatoid arthritis joint involvement.
vivas.a: SLE joints are non‑erosive, symmetrical, and often migratory; RA joints are erosive, asymmetrical, and persistent.

vivas.q: A patient on prednisone develops new shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. What is the likely diagnosis and immediate management?
vivas.a: Suspect pleuritis or pericarditis; perform chest X‑ray, ECG, and echocardiogram; start high‑dose steroids and colchicine if pericarditis.

vivas.q: What laboratory finding is commonly associated with intrinsic AKI due to post‑infectious glomerulonephritis or SLE?
vivas.a: Low C3/C4 with normal C1q and positive anti‑dsDNA.

vivas.q: Which autoantibody strongly suggests SLE over other autoimmune diseases?
vivas.a: Anti‑dsDNA and anti‑Smith antibodies are highly specific for SLE.

vivas.q: Why is high‑dose steroids not absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy?
vivas.a: They are used for severe flares; benefits outweigh risks if necessary, but avoid prolonged high doses.

vivas.q: What is the paradoxical effect of lupus anticoagulant in vivo?
vivas.a: It increases thrombosis risk despite prolonging in vitro coagulation assays.

vivas.q: What is the most common cardiac manifestation in SLE?
vivas.a: Libman–Sacks endocarditis (non‑bacterial verrucous lesions on valves).

vivas.q: How would you differentiate SLE pleuritis from TB pleuritis in a low‑resource setting?
vivas.a: Look for fever, night sweats, weight loss, and history of TB; pleural fluid ADA >40 IU/L suggests TB; low ADA favors SLE.

vivas.q: What is the key management step for a patient with SLE and new onset proteinuria?
vivas.a: Screen for lupus nephritis: urine protein/creatinine ratio, renal function, anti‑dsDNA, complement; refer to nephrology if nephritis suspected.

vivas.q: Why is mycophenolate contraindicated in pregnancy?
vivas.a: It is teratogenic, causing fetal malformations; switch to azathioprine if needed.

vivas.q: What is the most common cause of morbidity and mortality in SLE?
vivas.a: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of mortality; renal failure is a major morbidity.

mcqs.q: A 30‑year‑old woman with SLE presents with fever, arthralgia, and a malar rash. ANA is 1:640. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
mcqs.e: Anti‑dsDNA and complement assess disease activity.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of lupus nephritis?
mcqs.e: Lupus nephritis does not cause erosive arthritis.

mcqs.q: A patient with SLE has a positive lupus anticoagulant. What is the clinical implication?
Which of the following is a common cardiovascular complication of SLE?

cases.v: 45‑year‑old woman with SLE on hydroxychloroquine presents with new onset dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, and low‑grade fever. Chest X‑ray shows bilateral pleural effusions.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
What is the first investigation you would order?
qs.a: Echocardiogram to rule out pericarditis and assess effusion size.
High‑dose oral prednisone and colchicine; consider diuretics if fluid overload.

cases.v: 22‑year‑old pregnant woman with SLE (on hydroxychloroquine) develops proteinuria (protein/creatinine ratio 2.5) and hypertension.

qs.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
qs.a: Screen for lupus nephritis: urine microscopy, anti‑dsDNA, complement, and renal ultrasound.

qs.q: Which medication should be avoided during pregnancy?
What is the target blood pressure in pregnancy for this patient?

mistakes: Assuming ANA positivity alone confirms SLE; requires ≥10 points in 2019 criteria.
Treating mild SLE with high‑dose steroids; should use hydroxychloroquine and NSAIDs first.
Ignoring low complement levels as non‑specific; they indicate active disease.
Prescribing mycophenolate in pregnancy; it is teratogenic.
Overlooking lupus anticoagulant as a pro‑thrombotic marker.
Misinterpreting pleural effusion as TB without ADA testing.
Using cyclophosphamide in pregnancy without specialist input.
Failing to monitor renal function in SLE patients with proteinuria.

A 28‑year‑old woman with malar rash, arthralgia, and fatigue has a positive ANA. What is the next step? — Order anti‑dsDNA, complement levels, and renal screen (urine protein/creatinine).
Why is hydroxychloroquine preferred over azathioprine in stable SLE? — Hydroxychloroquine reduces flares, is safe in pregnancy, and has fewer myelosuppressive effects.
Explain the difference between SLE and rheumatoid arthritis joint involvement. — SLE joints are non‑erosive, symmetrical, and often migratory; RA joints are erosive, asymmetrical, and persistent.

A patient on prednisone develops new shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. What is the likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Suspect pleuritis or pericarditis; perform chest X‑ray, ECG, and echocardiogram; start high‑dose steroids and colchicine if pericarditis.
What laboratory finding is commonly associated with intrinsic AKI due to post‑infectious glomerulonephritis or SLE? — Low C3/C4 with normal C1q and positive anti‑dsDNA.
Which autoantibody strongly suggests SLE over other autoimmune diseases? — Anti‑dsDNA and anti‑Smith antibodies are highly specific for SLE.
Why is high‑dose steroids not absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy? — They are used for severe flares; benefits outweigh risks if necessary, but avoid prolonged high doses.
What is the paradoxical effect of lupus anticoagulant in vivo? — It increases thrombosis risk despite prolonging in vitro coagulation assays.
What is the most common cardiac manifestation in SLE? — Libman–Sacks endocarditis (non‑bacterial verrucous lesions on valves).

How would you differentiate SLE pleuritis from TB pleuritis in a low‑resource setting? — Look for fever, night sweats, weight loss, and history of TB; pleural fluid ADA >40 IU/L suggests TB; low ADA favors SLE.

What is the key management step for a patient with SLE and new onset proteinuria? — Screen for lupus nephritis: urine protein/creatinine ratio, renal function, anti‑dsDNA, complement; refer to nephrology if nephritis suspected.
Why is mycophenolate contraindicated in pregnancy? — It is teratogenic, causing fetal malformations; switch to azathioprine if needed.
